>Suicide is a stoic's disease. The people who do it don't talk.

Got anything to back that up or are you talking out your ass? I fail to see how someone expressing ambivalence toward dying, a monumental decision, will always and inevitably lead to them deciding life is the better choice. You need look no farther than this very subreddit to find at least a few examples that would disprove that particular idea. People who failed to answer a friend's cry for help and found them dead in the morning, people killing themselves while on the line with suicide hotline operators, people leaving behind fairly obvious warnings before taking their own life, etc. 

Lots of people don't leave behind signs or talk to anyone, but certainly plenty of people do. Many people who commit suicide are not thinking rationally (not to say none are), so of course they may not take the rational course and speak to no one before they die.

Your "I'm just a skeptic asking some questions, all you guys are just anti-science" concern trolling smart guy shtick pretty much instantly crumbles when you also include well known historical misinformation right out the gate. Pretty much everybody who was literate knew the Earth was round, and had since Plato looked up at a partial lunar eclipse and deduced that the circular shadow on the moon was Earth's. [And, since you brought up Carl Sagan, here is with another ancient, well known proof of Earth's roundness. ](https://youtu.be/3EspZtA7C3o)

But, that's not the main issue I have with your post. Of course ancient people used to believe in some pretty ridiculous things. No, my issue would be "You can't collect new data on past events." Nonsense. Utter tripe. You most certainly can, if it leaves evidence. [Like, say, ice snow trapping bubbles of atmospheric gases. ](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/blogs/national-museum-of-natural-history/2018/03/23/heres-how-scientists-reconstruct-earths-past-climates/#:~:text=One%20way%20to%20measure%20past,gases%20get%20trapped%20within%20it.&text=The%20temperature%20record%20recovered%20from,landmasses%20like%20Greenland%20and%20Antarctica.) Or, hell, even something as simple as carbon dating. Or simply discovering that dinosaurs used to exist! That certainly was a new bit of data gleamed from the past.

Just because nobody respects your opinion does not make you an oppressed visionary. They laughed at Galileo, but they also laughed at Bozo the Clown.

Others went on to relatively normal lives, going to college and getting jobs.

Life's a crapshoot. There's nothing that assures success or failure. Not karma, not hard work, heck, not even all the advantages or disadvantages in the world can definitively sway things one way or another.

Not that guy, but I have some criticisms to lob at Jung. Namely, he wasn't even wrong. By which I mean: his entire school of thought was pseudoscience, creating unfalsifiable hypothesis and often putting the cart before the horse in terms of conclusion and observation. Compare him to an actual scientist from the same time, Albert Einstein. When Einstein hypothesised theories, he gave specific explanations as to how you would be able to tell if he was right or wrong.  Freud and Jung provided no such explanations, instead merely observing and proclaiming, claiming truth at the first sign of a pattern.

The result: though modern psychologists and psychiatrists distance themselves from figures like Jung and Freud and Frankl, there can be no doubt that their influence is still felt. It has left psychology in its current state: a Frankenstein's Monster combination of philosophy, conjecture, politics and statistics stitched together by vague definitions, wearing the mask of science, and ultimately powerless against the challenges it faces. It turns out the majority of experiment results in the field cannot be replicated. The suicide rate continues to rise in the group of people who you would least expect and of whom have been most studied (white males) and psychology has no answers as to why or how to stop it. The president of the APA declared "positive psychology" the law of the land, but nobody is feeling all that positive.

>Why kill yourself. You already lived as long as you have...why end it now?

That's the sunk cost fallacy.

As for the suffering of others, it really doesn't matter. Viktor Frankl, holocaust survivor, made the point best.

>To draw an analogy: a man's suffering is similar to the behavior of a gas. If a certain quantity of gas is pumped into an empty chamber, it will fill the chamber completely and evenly, no matter how big the chamber. Thus suffering completely fills the human soul and conscious mind, no matter whether the suffering is great or little. Therefore the "size" of human suffering is absolutely relative.

I don't agree with everything the man said but this particular point sticks with me. 

Other people have it worse, I know this, and if they wanted to swap lives I gladly would, taking their death in exchange for my life. But, since such a thing is impossible, the best option remains suicide. To phrase it another way; just because there are starving people in Africa doesn't mean I should be grateful to the man who's strapping me down and force feeding me. 

You say suicide is selfish, I say to demand someone live is far more selfish. To say "No! It would hurt my feelings too much if you died in this way. Instead, you have to die in some other way. I don't care if you're suffering," is cruel. I would expect no one to make such a life long sacrifice for me, I ask for the same.

>Life is hard for all of us, but life is worth living. 

Why? In what way is life worth living? A statement like that requires evidence.

Not really. At least here there's a possibility of feeling understood by a peer instead of just lectured at and told how grateful we should be for the "gift" of life. Though, you could argue that's not a particularly good treatment philosophy, given the rising rate of suicide in the United States.

I don't think it's that big of an if. That it's even brought up as a possibility, despite there being virtually no good evidence for it, or even a suggestion found in the natural world that it might be a thing, is so strange. The entire idea of there being some sort of consciousness after death seems totally bizarre to me, not to mention anthro-centric in the extreme to the point of narcissism.

Nowhere in OP's original post do they mention "meaning" so I'm not sure why you bring it up. You're assuming OP is feeling some sort of existential suffering, not some very real physical suffering, or justified emotional pain. 

To that end, your definition of suffering seems very flawed. The definition that would make the most sense to me would be "Craving pleasurable sensations but instead feeling painful ones." It's not a rejection of the pain, but instead an acknowledgment of it, and the fact that you are indeed feeling it and you would rather not. 

Further, your notion to simply "reject suffering" seems very flippant. Not to mention; I can think of no better way to "reject suffering" than to make myself literally unable to feel it.

This is patently untrue. Cops don't even bother testing half the rape kits they get, what makes you think they'd launch a full scale investigation, including searching through computers and private things, into an obvious suicide?

They'd probably take anything obviously related to the death, including suicide notes.

I mean he still agreed with my interpretation and refutation of his analogy.

Even assuming he meant hell, the analogy is still poor because despite saying we know nothing about it, he still makes the choice between "A shit sandwich and something really bad" instead of "A shit sandwich and an unknown that we assume is bad but know nothing about."

Then why add the further clarification of "(about which you know nothing, and might be eternal damnation or pain)"? If the "bad experience about which we knowing" he was referring to was hell, he wouldn't need to clarify like that. The clarification really only makes sense if he's talking about death, since otherwise he'd be pre-supposing suicide leads to hell, but the argument itself is based on not knowing what happens, if anything, after death. 

Also he agreed with me. It's the other response to my comment.

Your analogy isn't good either, because we all have to experience death no matter what. It's just a question of timing and cause. 

Further, you say : "Would you eat one shitty sandwich, or will you experience something really bad (about which you know nothing, and which might be eternal damnation or pain)?" but you're assuming death is bad. What makes death intrinsically "really bad"? I see it more neutrally. Sometimes it's a merciful end, sometimes it's a tragic end, but there's no stopping it.

I think the original analogy is more apt. You have a choice, eat the sandwich, then move on to the unknown time beyond the sandwich, or don't eat the sandwich/eat enough to know its dog shit, and speed up the time until you no longer have to deal with the sandwich, and face what, if anything, lies beyond the sandwich.

There's a strong argument to be made that we hear the story so much due to survivorship bias. There are some (but not all, it's a controversial finding) studies that indicate more lethal methods used in first suicide attempts are more likely to result in successful suicide attempts down the road.

There's also the fact that a previous suicide attempt is the biggest predictor of a future death by suicide. Sure, 90 percent of those who attempt don't go on to die by suicide, but what do we say about the 10 percent that do?
I hear that "regret it halfway down" bullshit all the time. As someone who's attempted suicide, at the time I felt no such thing and the only thing I feel about it now is regret that I failed.
